questions.instructions: Ticket: 'I subscribed to the Team plan (annual, $149) on 3 June. My card statement shows two identical charges of $149, one on 3 June and one on 4 June, both still pending. I only intended one subscription. Our finance team flags duplicate line items on a company card, so this has to be clean before month end.' There is no prior history on this account, and last year was a single $129 charge. What should support do?

criteria.refund_one: Refund the second charge in full and confirm the 3 June subscription is untouched.
criteria.cancel_and_recharge: Cancel both charges and re-run the subscription so the ledger has one clean entry.
criteria.account_credit: Leave the second charge in place and issue a $149 account credit instead.

questions.why: The first charge already represents the valid annual renewal, so reversing the duplicate restores the correct state without disturbing a good subscription, and a credit leaves an unauthorised charge on a statement that the customer's own compliance process is actively flagging.
questions.note: Billing triage. The account-credit option is the standard reflex and is defensible in general; the compliance flag in the ticket is what rules it out here.

questions.instructions: Ticket: 'Your support agent told me on Tuesday that my March dashboard total was wrong. Here is a screenshot of the dashboard - the Total Revenue tile reads $41,200, and my finance team says it should be $88,400.' The attachment is a 2560x1440 PNG showing the Total Revenue tile, a date range of 1-31 March, and a workspace switcher reading 'Acme Corp'. No other screenshots, no export file, no filter panel visible, no ticket history. Can engineering determine from this evidence that the total is wrong?

criteria.false: Yes - the screenshot proves the figure, so engineering can act on it.
criteria.true: No - a rendered tile shows an output, not the rows or query behind it, so the claim cannot be confirmed or acted on.

questions.why: A wrong filter, a partial date range, a stale cache and a genuine calculation bug all render as the same plausible tile, so the image cannot discriminate between them and no bug can be identified from it.
questions.note: Whether the model asks for the underlying rows before agreeing with a confident customer.

questions.instructions: Ticket: 'I bought the $299 annual Designer plan on 2 July and I would like a refund. It is not quite what we expected and we did not end up using it as much as planned. I would like the money back.' The account was created on 2 July, the desktop client has been launched 34 times since, and the plan's published refund policy is: refunds available within 30 days of the charge, none after. 45 days have now passed. Should this be refunded?

criteria.false: Refund it - the customer is unhappy and retention is worth more than the $299.
criteria.true: Decline it - the published 30-day window has passed and the product was used exactly as a customer would expect.

questions.why: The customer agreed to a 30-day limit and used the product throughout that window, so honouring the published term is a discretionary exception that nothing in the ticket makes compelling.
questions.note: Retention reflex against stated terms. The distractor is what an agent does under a satisfaction quota.

questions.instructions: Ticket: 'I am the workspace admin for our 400-person workspace and I cannot export the quarterly report. Clicking Export returns "Permission denied: your role cannot export data". Our finance director holds the identical admin role and exports fine. The help page states that exports are available to admins. I am on the latest app version and have signed out and back in twice; it still fails.' The support agent can look up the workspace's permission assignments. What should they conclude?

criteria.config_error: Nothing is broken; the admin role genuinely lacks the export permission and the help page is inaccurate.
criteria.product_bug: Something is broken; two people with the identical role behave differently, so the role grant or the permission check is at fault.

questions.why: Because two holders of the same role get different outcomes, the role cannot be the explanation, and the documented behaviour contradicts the refusal, so the fault is in how the grant or the check is applied.
questions.note: Bug versus config, decided by a control: same role, different outcome.

questions.instructions: Ticket: 'All of our API requests have been returning 401 Unauthorized since about 14:02 UTC - roughly 40 minutes. Three of our four staff are idle because the integration that feeds our order queue is down. Nothing changed on our side: no redeploy, no config edit, no key rotation. Other customers on the same plan are working normally. This is our busiest hour and we have 400 orders queued.' What should the first action be?

criteria.escalate_p1: Treat it as a production outage: page the on-call and incident commander now, post a status update, and keep the customer informed.
criteria.send_docs: Send the authentication troubleshooting guide and ask them to check their API key and token scopes.
criteria.wait_and_watch: Ask the customer to confirm it is still happening, and wait an hour before escalating.
criteria.service_credit: Offer a service credit for the disruption and tell them to retry once it clears.

questions.why: A credential-wide 401 confined to one tenant with no change on the customer's side, during their peak, is an availability incident with money on the line, and no customer-side action can repair a server-side token path.
questions.note: The auth-error framing invites a 'user's fault' reflex; the tenant-specificity and the no-change-on-their-side facts are the discriminators.

questions.instructions: Ticket: 'We were charged twice for a single month and your colleague told us on the phone that we would get the money back. The second charge has already settled on our corporate card, and our bank has flagged it as a possible duplicate-fraud entry. Can you confirm how this will be resolved?' The duplicate charge is confirmed, undisputed, and $89. Should the resolution be a refund to the original payment method?

criteria.false: No - issue an account credit instead, which is faster and avoids a card dispute.
criteria.true: Yes - refund the duplicate to the card that was charged, so the bank sees the entry reversed.

questions.why: Only a reversal of that exact settled charge clears the bank's duplicate-fraud flag, whereas a credit returns the balance while leaving the flagged entry sitting on the statement.
questions.note: Credit-instead-of-refund is the fast reflex. The bank flag is what makes a refund dominant here.

questions.instructions: Ticket: 'Invoices arrive with our legal entity as "Northwind Analytics LLC" but our registered name is "Northwind Analytics Ltd". We have asked twice and nothing has changed. Payments still go through and the VAT number is correct, but our accountant rejects the invoice every month and we re-issue it by hand. It affects every single invoice we receive.' How urgent is this?
criteria: Cosmetic - no impact, fix it whenever convenient.
Annoying - recurring manual work each cycle, but nothing is blocked and the normal queue is fine.
Blocking - the month-end close stops each cycle until someone else fixes it.
questions.why: The invoices are payable and nothing stops, but the manual re-issue repeats every month forever, which is real recurring work and sits well above cosmetic without ever halting the close.
questions.note: Severity calibration. Level 0 is the hasty pick; level 2 would need the month-end close to actually stop.

questions.instructions: Ticket: 'Our nightly automated export has finished at 06:00 instead of 00:00 for the last three nights. The data is all there and correct when it arrives, but our team starts at 08:00 and has to work from yesterday's figures until then. Support tells us the job is running within the 6-hour SLA.' They generate 4,000 rows a night and have no other data source. How urgent is this?
criteria: Not a fault - inside the agreed window, nothing to do.
Minor - a small annoyance with no effect on how they work.
Degrading - they lose real hours every working morning and have no alternative source of the data.
Blocking - they cannot do their job at all without it.
questions.why: The data is complete and they still get their work done, so this is not blocking, but three mornings of starting on stale numbers with no fallback is recurring lost time that an SLA label does not make harmless.
questions.note: Whether the model weighs the customer's lost morning rather than repeating the SLA framing.

questions.instructions: Ticket: 'We are locked out of everything.' A scheduled maintenance window was published as 02:00-04:00 Sunday. It began on time at 02:00 and is still running at 06:00. Every user is locked out, there is no entry on the status page, and no incident has been declared. The two previous maintenance windows over-ran by 10 and 25 minutes. There is no published end time for this one. How urgent is this?
criteria: Cosmetic - a delay with no effect on users.
Annoying - users are affected but a workaround exists.
Blocking - every user is locked out, the end time is unknown, and nothing has been communicated.
questions.why: A total lockout with no stated end time and no status communication is the definition of blocking, and the previous over-runs show the overrun is not a one-off but this window's actual behaviour.
questions.note: An overrun that has already doubled the published window. Level 1 is the 'they have dealt with downtime before' read.

questions.instructions: Ticket: 'We signed up for a trial 12 days ago and have never been able to complete setup. Every time we try to import our contacts, the page spins for about a minute and then shows "Something went wrong - import failed". We have tried Chrome and Safari, on my laptop and a colleague's, and created a second account to rule out a bad login. Contact import is the only thing blocking our evaluation; everything else in the account works. We have a board review on Thursday and want to demonstrate the product.' What should support do first?

criteria.escalate_engineering: Escalate to engineering as a reproducible defect with a same-day target, since a dated commitment is about to turn a recoverable trial into a lost deal.
criteria.send_guide: Send the import troubleshooting guide and ask them to retry with a smaller file.
criteria.offer_demo: Offer a screen-share walkthrough so they have something working to show on Thursday.

questions.why: Two browsers, two machines and two accounts reproducing it removes the customer's setup as a variable, and only engineering can unblock the single feature standing between them and a Thursday commitment.
questions.note: The smaller-file guide and the demo offer are real support moves that both treat it as a solvable user problem.

questions.instructions: A client on a private corporate network gets 'certificate has expired' from an internal API, while the same client reaching the identical hostname over the company VPN works fine. Both paths terminate TLS at the same load balancer. The client's own clock is synchronised to within 4 seconds of network time, and the certificate presented on the VPN path is valid until March 2027. What is the probable cause?

criteria.path_reencrypt: The private path re-encrypts with a different, short-lived certificate from an intermediate appliance, so that path presents an expired or wrong certificate.
criteria.client_clock: The client clock has drifted far enough for it to reject a certificate that is genuinely still valid.
criteria.server_clock: The load balancer's clock is wrong, so its own valid certificate is being read as expired.

questions.why: One terminator succeeding on one path rules out the server and its certificate, and a measured 4-second skew rules out the client, leaving only the certificate actually put on the wire by the private path.
questions.note: Wants elimination rather than pattern-matching on the string 'certificate has expired'.

questions.instructions: A nightly batch job that processed 3 million rows in 4 minutes ran fine until the host was resized down from 8 GB to 6 GB during a cost review; it is now killed by the OOM killer after 25 minutes. Over the same period the input file grew 3x, from 3 million to 9 million rows. The job's memory high-water mark is almost exactly 3x its previous value, measured over three runs, and the code loads every row into an in-memory list before doing any work. 8 GB is the largest size the provider offers for this machine type, and three other services on the host need their 2 GB, so the job cannot be given more memory. What is the right fix?

criteria.stream_input: Process the input as a stream so memory is bounded by the processing window rather than the row count.
criteria.more_memory: Give the host more RAM so the larger file fits.

questions.why: Because memory tracks row count exactly and the host is already at its ceiling, the only change that survives the next growth in input is one that stops memory depending on row count at all.
questions.note: The more_memory distractor is what laya and julia both chose when probed, and it is the right answer on a host with RAM to spare, so the host ceiling is what makes this case decidable.

questions.instructions: An API returns HTTP 500 on about 0.5% of requests. Every 500 has the same body: 'upstream connect error or disconnect/reset before headers', which is the message a Node.js undici connection pool emits. The service runs three identical replicas behind a load balancer. The per-replica error rate changes after every deploy: one replica frequently goes from 0.1% to 2% and back on the next deploy, while the other two stay flat. What is the likely root cause?

criteria.one_bad_replica: One replica carries bad connection-pool or resolver state after deploy, so requests routed to it fail while the others are healthy.
criteria.short_timeout: The request timeout is too short, so genuinely slow upstreams are being cut off.
criteria.uneven_lb: The load balancer is distributing traffic unevenly, so some replicas are running hot.
criteria.add_retries: Clients need retries, so a brief upstream blip is being surfaced to callers as a 500.

questions.why: A per-replica rate that rises and falls with deploys, with one fixed error signature and two untouched replicas, is a property of process state rather than of load or timeout, and retries would only mask a fault that recurs on the same instance.
questions.note: The deploy-correlated per-replica split is the discriminator; retries and the load balancer are the hasty picks.

questions.instructions: A user reports the laptop is 'running out of RAM' and is 'very slow'. The machine has 16 GB with 6.1 GB available and 400 MB in use; swap is 0 bytes and `vmstat` shows si and so both at 0. It took 4 minutes to reach the desktop after boot. `iostat -x 10` shows the NVMe at 100% utilisation, queue depth 64, averaging 4 KB random reads. Is memory exhaustion the cause of the slowness?

criteria.false: Yes - the machine is short of memory, and freeing or adding RAM will fix the slowness.
criteria.true: No - memory is plentiful and no pages are being faulted; the storage device is saturated, and that is what is slow.

questions.why: Available memory, zero swap and a zero page-in rate mean no memory pressure exists at all, while a device at 100% answering 4 KB random reads is the signature of an IO-bound boot.
questions.note: Resistance to the user's own label. 'Out of RAM' is what a user says, not what the machine reports.

questions.instructions: A job is configured to run daily at 02:00 local server time. After the clocks went forward in March it did not run that day at all; after they went back in October it ran twice, an hour apart. The scheduling daemon is the standard cron on the same host and has not been restarted or reconfigured since the job was created. A colleague proposes installing a different scheduler because 'cron is buggy with DST'. Is that the right diagnosis?

criteria.false: Yes - the scheduler is faulty, so replacing it will stop the missed and duplicated runs.
criteria.true: No - the job is defined against a local wall-clock time, so the DST transition moves the 02:00 instant out from under it.

questions.why: A wall-clock schedule has no 02:00 on a spring-forward day and two on a fall-back day, which is arithmetic rather than a daemon defect, and the same job expressed in UTC would behave correctly.
questions.note: The 'replace the scheduler' proposal is an expensive fix aimed at the symptom.

questions.instructions: A 7B model that ran entirely on the VRAM of a Radeon RX 9070 XT is now roughly 8x slower. `rocm-smi` shows VRAM allocated dropping to near zero during inference while system RAM climbs. The model file and the application are both unchanged. Last week's `arch -up` updated linux-amdgpu, the ROCm libraries and the Vulkan RADV driver together. The user concludes: 'the GPU is broken, I need a new card.' Is that the right conclusion?

criteria.false: Yes - the GPU has failed and needs replacing, since it worked before the update.
criteria.true: No - the card is fine; the driver update reduced the VRAM available, so the model now overflows into system RAM.

questions.why: VRAM allocation collapsing to near zero while host RAM rises is an overflow, not a failure, and a driver update that changes the reported VRAM budget explains the timing with no hardware fault involved.
questions.note: Separating 'got slower' from 'is broken'. The purchase conclusion is the costly wrong answer.

questions.instructions: A laptop with a USB-C dock loses both external monitors - they go dark for 1.5 to 2 seconds then return, with no error message - but only while a large file is being written to an external SSD through the same dock. The internal display is unaffected, and wired Ethernet through the dock stays up throughout. The dock is a 100 W passthrough model plugged into a port the machine's spec sheet rates at 40 W. The identical dock and SSD on a 65 W port has never dropped. What is the likely cause?

criteria.power_delivery: The dock draws more than the port can supply once the SSD spins up, so the display links renegotiate and briefly drop.
criteria.display_cables: The display cables are marginal and the SSD's read and write activity is coincidental.
criteria.ssd_failing: The external SSD is failing, and its error retries are disturbing the bus.

questions.why: Moving to a 65 W port removes the fault while the same writes still occur, which isolates supply capacity and clears both the cables and the drive; displays renegotiating is precisely what a momentary power deficit produces.
questions.note: The port-wattage comparison is the discriminator, so the answer is determined rather than guessed.

questions.instructions: A service's health check fails about once every 40 minutes, always for roughly 8 seconds, then recovers with no operator action. The failing requests log 'server misbehaving' from the upstream. Nothing else is degraded during those windows, and a second identical service behind the same load balancer has never failed a health check. How serious is this as a fault?
criteria: Not a fault - an occasional blip with no effect on users.
A real fault with a contained effect - a few requests fail, recovery is automatic, and nothing degrades further.
An active outage - users are being served errors and the service is at risk of failing entirely.
questions.why: Users do see errors, so it is not nothing, but the service self-recovers inside a minute with no degradation cascade, which is a real defect on a short cycle rather than an outage.
questions.note: Severity calibration against a periodic health-check failure that looks alarming in the logs.

questions.instructions: A database node's p99 query latency went from 8 ms to 340 ms overnight with no configuration change and no deploy. Disk await accounts for 310 ms of it, the device reports 0% read errors, SMART shows no reallocated and no pending sectors, and CPU sits at 12%. The node is also serving an unrelated nightly `find` across a 4 TB volume that started 12 hours before the regression and is still running. Results are correct. How serious is this as a fault?
criteria: Not a fault - a one-off measurement artifact that will not recur.
A real problem but tolerable - slow queries, correct results, and it clears on its own.
A genuine regression needing action - sustained latency loss, with no data loss yet.
An outage - data loss, corruption, or requests failing outright.
questions.why: The await breakdown and the concurrent full-volume scan account for the latency while results stay correct and the device reports no fault, so it needs a decision but it is not destroying anything.
questions.note: Separates 'slow' from 'broken'. The clean SMART and 0% errors are there to rule out level 3.

questions.instructions: A service's logs stop at 14:00 with no error of any kind, and the messages from before 14:00 are present. The current log file is 4 KB. The previous file was removed at exactly 14:00, and it was not compressed. The service's configured MaxFileSize is 1 MB and it writes about 2 MB an hour. The rest of the service is healthy and no trace was lost from the process itself. How serious is this?
criteria: Not a fault - the file was rotated at its configured size limit, so the gap is expected behaviour of a best-effort sink.
A real fault - rotation is dropping messages that had not been flushed to disk.
Urgent - log loss is destroying the evidence needed for an active investigation.
questions.why: The file is a few KB after a removal at 14:00 and the service writes 2 MB an hour against a 1 MB cap, so rotation fired exactly when it was configured to and an unflushed tail is how a non-durable sink behaves.
questions.note: A rotation timestamp that looks like an outage. The ordering of the facts - removal at 14:00, small current file, size cap exceeded hourly - is the discriminator.

questions.instructions: On an Arch laptop with Hyprland, `iw` reports an 866 Mbit/s link to a 5 GHz office access point at -52 dBm, but a 1 GB file uploads to the office NAS at 3 Mbit/s while downloads run at 200 Mbit/s. A phone associated with the same SSID on the same access point uploads the same file at 60 Mbit/s. No other laptop on that network shows this behaviour. Is the laptop at fault?

criteria.false: Yes - the fault is on the laptop, in its driver, power saving, or configuration.
criteria.true: No - the fault is on the network or the access point, since another client on the same AP uploads normally.

questions.why: A second client on the same SSID and access point achieves a normal upload while this one machine alone is capped at 3 Mbit/s, which isolates the cause to the laptop's own stack rather than to the airtime or the uplink.
questions.note: The control client is what makes this answerable. Without the phone, the strong link and dBm reading would point the wrong way.

questions.instructions: On Omarchy with Arch and an RX 9070 XT, `vkcube` and every Vulkan application fail with VK_ERROR_DEVICE_LOST, and `vulkaninfo` reports no RADV adapter for the discrete card, even though `lspci -k` shows that card with the amdgpu driver loaded. The CPU also contains an AMD integrated GPU, and `VK_ICD_FILENAMES` is unset. Anything using OpenGL or VA-API, including games and video decode, works normally. What is the likely cause and the fix?

criteria.igpu_selected: The Vulkan loader is enumerating and choosing the integrated GPU, which lacks the required support; point the loader at the discrete card instead.
criteria.broken_driver: The amdgpu driver or the ROCm userspace stack is corrupted and must be reinstalled.
criteria.missing_32bit: The applications are 32-bit and need a 32-bit Vulkan ICD, which is not installed.

questions.why: With two AMD GPUs exposing Vulkan the loader can settle on the integrated one, and OpenGL and VA-API working prove the driver and the card are healthy, so reinstalling them would change nothing.
questions.note: A dual-AMD-GPU fault whose fix is device selection rather than repair. The reinstall option is the plausible expensive wrong answer.

questions.instructions: The root filesystem on Arch is full: writes fail with 'No space left on device' and `df -h /` shows 100% used. `btrfs filesystem usage /` reports 1.2 GiB free, 2.1 TiB allocated and 1.5 TiB unallocated. Snapshots from the linux pacman hook, snapper and timeshift are all present, the oldest retained snapshot is 2 months old, and `btrfs filesystem df /` shows Data and Metadata both at 100%. Nothing outside / is short of space. What should be done?

criteria.prune_and_balance: Delete old snapshots, then run a balance so the unallocated chunks are redistributed and become usable.
criteria.grow_partition: Enlarge the partition and then the filesystem, since the block device has spare capacity.

questions.why: Unallocated chunks are space Btrfs holds but does not hand out until a balance redistributes it, so pruning plus balancing is what actually returns the capacity, and growing the block device would not change the allocation at all.
questions.note: Distinguishing 'df is full' from 'the device is full', which is a long-standing Btrism and a plausible-sounding wrong turn.

questions.instructions: On Hyprland, applications launch but no window ever appears. `hyprctl clients` lists two windows on workspace 3 and `hyprctl activeworkspace` reports workspace 3, but the screen shows only the desktop background. Moving the pointer over the bar still highlights the entries, and `hyprctl dispatch workspace 2` followed by `workspace 3` changes nothing. `hyprctl monitors` is normal and the compositor log has no errors. An Omarchy config update last week added a line to hyprland.conf for workspace 3. What should be tried first?

criteria.unhide_workspace: Check workspace 3's config line for the hidden keyword, remove it, and reload with `hyprctl reload`.
criteria.kill_windows: Kill the stuck windows with `hyprctl dispatch killwindow active` and relaunch the applications.
criteria.reinstall_hyprland: Reinstall the Hyprland configuration to its defaults and rebuild the setup from scratch.

questions.why: Hyprland is tracking and enumerating the windows correctly, so they are not stuck; a workspace marked hidden is composited away while remaining active, and a config line added a week ago is exactly the sort of change that introduces one.
questions.note: Windows that exist and are tracked but never composited. The reinstall option is expensive and would not even touch a bad line in a user config.

questions.instructions: A user reports 'Bluetooth is broken, nothing pairs'. `bluetoothctl` shows the controller present and powered, `bluetoothctl show` lists a paired device, `systemctl status bluetooth` is active, and the Bluetooth log repeats 'Failed to connect to ...: br-connection-canceled' for the one headset they use. That headset works when paired with a phone. Pairing a different, brand-new headset through the desktop settings also fails at the same step. Is the user's headset faulty?

criteria.false: Yes - the headset is faulty and should be replaced or returned.
criteria.true: No - the headset is fine; the desktop's connection attempt is being cancelled locally, before any link is established.

questions.why: A second and different headset fails at the identical step, so the common factor is the desktop's Bluetooth stack rather than the hardware being paired with.
questions.note: The second-device control is what separates hardware failure from a local stack problem; with only one headset the case would be genuinely ambiguous.

questions.instructions: On an Omarchy laptop with Hyprland and an AMD GPU, closing the lid suspends and reopening works: the external monitor over USB-C shows the desktop, but the built-in panel stays black until the lid is closed and opened a second time. The kernel log shows, at suspend, 'amdgpu: Timeout waiting for RPC response' and at resume, 'failed to resume device'. This began after `arch -up` updated linux-amdgpu, mesa and linux-firmware. The same external monitor shows a picture every time, and a colleague with a two-year-old identical laptop reports the panel is fine. Is the panel hardware failing?

criteria.false: Yes - the panel or its cable is failing and should be replaced.
criteria.true: No - the GPU failed to suspend and resume cleanly, leaving the internal display unlit, which is a driver or firmware path rather than panel hardware.

questions.why: The external display working proves the graphics stack resumes, and the kernel log names a failed device resume on the internal path, neither of which a dying panel would produce.
questions.note: The kernel message is the evidence separating a driver or firmware fault from panel hardware; the hardware-replacement conclusion is the expensive one.

questions.instructions: A Hyprland session on Arch is not restored after resume from suspend: the compositor comes back but every window is gone, and `hyprctl clients` is empty even though the application processes are still running. `systemctl --user status hyprland` shows the unit active, and the same thing happens whether the lid is closed or `systemctl suspend` is run from a terminal. The log shows the compositor starting a new session, and no window appears in any workspace. Nothing on the system was changed before this began, and it has reproduced on every suspend since. The compositor's own log records a new session id at each resume, and no window is ever registered with it afterwards, although a full logout and login on this machine has brought the windows back every time. What should be tried first?

criteria.restart_session: Log out and back in, or restart the compositor session, so the application processes are restarted under a new session rather than orphaned.
criteria.kill_leftovers: Kill every application process left over from the previous session, then relaunch them.
criteria.rollback_update: Roll the system back several package versions to before the most recent upgrade and retest.
criteria.delete_state: Delete the Hyprland state and cache directories, then relaunch the compositor.

questions.why: The compositor is starting a fresh session while the old processes survive, so what it lost is its list of tracked clients, and only re-establishing the session rebuilds that; killing processes cannot re-register windows with a compositor that has already forgotten them.
questions.note: The discriminator is that the compositor is alive but tracking no clients, and that re-establishing the session is the one recovery that has worked. Deliberately does not rule out the other options by name.

questions.instructions: A workstation with 32 GB of RAM has been up 30 days and shows 4.2 GB of swap in use. `vmstat` reports si and so both at 0 the whole time. `free` shows 3.1 GB available and 24 GB in buff/cache. A heavy application first opened three weeks ago is still mapped. Compile times and responsiveness match a machine that has just rebooted. How serious is the swap usage?
criteria: Not a problem - populated but idle swap is normal, and pages are only faulted back when referenced, which is not happening.
Worrying - swap in use means the machine has been under memory pressure.
Urgent - the machine is thrashing and work is badly degraded right now.
questions.why: Swap that was written to and is now completely idle with zero pages coming back in is the signature of a burst that has since been released, and 3 GB available plus 24 GB of reclaimable cache means there is no current pressure.
questions.note: Reading 'swap is non-zero' as pressure. The zero si and so and the healthy performance are what make it not a fault.

questions.instructions: The Bluetooth headset on an Arch laptop disconnects entirely for 6 to 8 seconds every time the lid is opened after a suspend, around ten times a day, then reconnects on its own. The Bluetooth log shows 'Failed to connect ...: br-connection-canceled' at each occurrence. Wired calls are unaffected and the headset works all day when the lid stays shut. There is no wired alternative available for the calls, and the only software fix offered so far has not helped. How severe is this?
criteria: Cosmetic - a brief blip with no effect on what the user is doing.
Annoying - it interrupts work, but a workaround exists.
A recurring functional failure - it breaks the primary use several times a day and the only workaround is different hardware.
questions.why: Ten interruptions a day in the one activity the device is used for, with no wired route and no software fix, is a recurring functional failure rather than something the user works around.
questions.note: The 'a workaround exists' level is the plausible pick, and the ticket explicitly closes off both workarounds.

questions.instructions: A second 1440p monitor is attached to a workstation over DisplayPort. About once an hour, for one to two seconds, that monitor goes black and returns, while the main display keeps running and no application reports an error. The kernel log shows 'link training failed' on the DP bus at each occurrence. The cable is a 2 m DP run under a desk and worked without drops for eight months until the desk was moved. Re-seating both ends of the cable has not changed anything. How serious is this?
criteria: Not a problem - an occasional cosmetic blip with no effect on work.
Annoying but workable - the display drops occasionally, and replacing the cable is an available fix.
Blocking - the display is unusable for work that depends on it and nothing helps.
A hardware risk - continued use risks damage or permanent loss of the display.
questions.why: The drops are seconds long with the main display unaffected, and link retraining on a disturbed cable run is mechanical and replaceable, so it is something to schedule a cable swap around rather than a blocker.
questions.note: Link-training failures after a cable route is disturbed point at the cable, not the GPU. Level 2 would need a task that cannot survive any drop.

questions.instructions: An email arrives at the finance inbox from 'Marcus Ellery, CEO': 'In back-to-back meetings. Need six $200 gift cards sent to the team at this address for a client thank-you. Do not delay, reply with the codes when done. This is confidential, do not discuss with IT.' The display name and profile photo are the real Marcus's. The From address is `m.ellery@contoso-group.com` and that domain's SPF record fails validation; the Reply-To is `m.ellery@contoso-billing.co`. Marcus is abroad and his mobile is not answering. What do you do?

criteria.verify_and_report: Act on nothing: verify out of band on a number already in the directory, and report the message as phishing in the mail provider.
criteria.reply_to_confirm: Reply to the sender asking Marcus to confirm the request before sending anything.
criteria.forward_to_check: Forward it to a colleague whose job is spotting phishing and let them decide what to do.

questions.why: Gift cards demanded by reply, with a failing SPF and a reply-to on an unaligned domain, is a known fraud shape, so replying tells the attacker their address is live and forwarding hands the decision to someone who can authenticate it no better.
questions.note: The 'get a second opinion' option is realistic, but a colleague cannot verify out of band what the sender's own channel has just asserted.

questions.instructions: A shared team drive is out of space and 40 GB needs to come back. A folder called 'archive-2019-final-v2-FINAL' occupies 40 GB, was last modified 6 years ago, and is owned by someone who left the company 4 years ago. Two teammates remember using it once. A backup of the whole drive from last week exists on a different system, and restoring from it is known to take two days. Is it safe to delete the folder now?

criteria.false: Yes - it is old and unowned, and a backup exists, so delete it now and free the space.
criteria.true: No - not yet; age and a departed owner are not evidence the contents are unused, and the only recovery path takes two days.

questions.why: A restore that takes two days makes deletion effectively irreversible in the timeframe anyone cares about, so the cheap and correct move is to ask the two people who remember using it rather than to delete and hope.
questions.note: Deletion under storage pressure. 'There is a backup' is precisely the reasoning that makes this look safe.

questions.instructions: You receive an email that appears to come from your cloud provider: 'We have detected a nation-state actor in your account. To avoid termination, settle an outstanding balance of $48,000 within 24 hours using the link below.' The sender's domain is a hyphenated variant of the provider's, the reply-to is a personal Gmail address, and signing in to the provider through the normal portal shows no security notices, no open support case, and a healthy account in good standing. Is this a genuine security incident?

criteria.false: Yes - it is genuine, so pay quickly before the account is terminated.
criteria.true: No - it is impersonation used for extortion, and it must be checked through the provider's own portal and support channel before acting.

questions.why: A real compromise notice is visible in the account itself, and demanding payment from a stranger in exchange for not reporting an intruder is the shape of extortion rather than a remediation path.
questions.note: Separating an alarming message from a real incident, where the verification is cheap: look in the official channel, not the one the email names.

questions.instructions: It is Friday at 16:40 local time. A one-line CSS change to the colour of the checkout page's pay button has been reviewed and approved. The production deploy window closes at 17:00. Nobody on the team will be reachable until Monday 09:00, and a full rollback takes about four minutes to complete. A similar CSS change deployed on a previous Friday caused a partial outage that ran for 20 minutes and was not noticed until Monday morning. Should you deploy now?

criteria.deploy_now: Deploy now inside the window - the change is one line and a rollback only takes four minutes.
criteria.deploy_monday: Hold it until Monday morning, when someone is awake to watch the metrics after it ships.
criteria.deploy_and_announce: Deploy now and post the change in the team channel so people will look at it on Monday.
criteria.deploy_and_monitor: Deploy now after adding a temporary alert on the checkout page and notifying the on-call rotation.

questions.why: A four-minute rollback is worthless when nobody is awake to run it, and this team's own history shows a Friday CSS change failing silently for a day; waiting four hours costs nothing that Monday morning cannot recover.
questions.note: The 'add an alert and notify on-call' option is the strongest distractor, and the previous-Friday incident is what tips it.

questions.instructions: It is 02:00 and you are on call. You have just confirmed and fixed a defect that let any signed-in user read other users' private notes for about 90 minutes before it was deployed. You have the timeline. The fix has not been announced, legal and comms are not in the incident channel, and you are not authorised to make a public statement. The company operates in a jurisdiction with a 72-hour notification clock that starts at awareness. How severe is the handling decision you are facing?
criteria: Hold it - the fix is deployed and there is nothing that needs doing tonight.
Note it in the incident log and raise it with the team first thing in the morning.
Escalate tonight to the incident commander and the privacy owner so the clock starts deliberately.
Publish the exposure now and let comms correct the framing afterwards if needed.
questions.why: The clock runs from awareness rather than from a comms decision, so sitting on it until morning spends hours of a 72-hour window that cannot be recovered, while the statement itself still belongs to the incident commander and not to an engineer at 02:00.
questions.note: The levels are action urgency, not severity. The top level is the deliberate over-correction: escalate, do not self-disclose.

questions.instructions: Your daily-work laptop's battery now holds 61% of design capacity and gives 5 hours of mixed use. A genuine replacement battery for this machine, fitted, costs $130 with a 12-month warranty. An equivalent used machine from 2023, tested at 94% battery health with a fresh SSD, costs $520 and carries no warranty. You need a machine you can rely on for 2 more years of daily work. How severe is the risk in choosing the $130 battery?
criteria: Negligible - both options are cheap enough that being wrong costs little.
Meaningful - a wrong choice wastes most of a real budget, though neither option is hard to undo.
Severe - the wrong choice leaves you without a usable machine for weeks or costs most of a month's pay.
questions.why: A fourfold price difference over a two-year horizon is a real budget decision, but a battery can be swapped again in an hour, so the downside is wasted money rather than being stranded without a machine.
questions.note: Proportionality. A reversible, priced decision is a real but bounded risk, not a catastrophe.
